root_causes.description: Responses load entire relation collections (favoritedBy, followedBy) to compute a membership boolean and a count
List endpoints have no server-enforced bound on result size
Schema lacks indexes on foreign-key and sort columns used by hot reads
Exact whole-set count recomputed per list request, serially
Tag popularity aggregate recomputed per request
CPU-bound password hashing on the single event loop
No instrumentation of requests, queries, or event loop
Capacity configuration (process count, heap, pool) implicit
Write path split into sequential non-transactional round trips with uncapped per-tag work

findings.problem: Article and profile queries include favoritedBy: true and author.followedBy: true (full User rows) only to compute favorited/following booleans and favoritesCount; data loaded grows with popularity, not response size.
findings.performance_principle: Fetch only what the response needs; answer membership tests and counts in the datastore rather than transferring whole collections.

evidence.statement: Same include in getFeed, createArticle, getArticle, updateArticle, favorite/unfavorite (lines 139, 221, 252, 365, 580, 626) and comment authors (447, 503)
Mapper uses only .some() membership and .length; requested _count is ignored
Profile paths load full followedBy for a membership test
Rows per list request ~ page x (1 + favorites/article + followers/author); derived from include shape. No runtime evidence exists.

findings.conditions: Matters once popular articles/authors have favorites/followers in the hundreds or more relative to page size. No row-count evidence; join tables are append-only with no cap. Workload unknown, so confidence capped at Medium.

counter_evidence.statement: Prisma 4 batches each relation level into one query, so query count is constant per request (no N+1); cost is row volume
Searched for any cap on favorites/followers: none
Join tables indexed on both columns, so relation queries are index lookups

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: At demo/seed scale (at most 12 favoriters/followers per item) the extra rows are trivial.
findings.recommendation: Use _count for favoritesCount and include favoritedBy/followedBy filtered to the current user id with select {id:true} (skip for anonymous requests); apply to profile queries too.

alternatives.why: Bounded to at most one row per relation per item, no schema change, removes the work

findings.trade_offs: Mapper signatures change; anonymous and authenticated requests use different query shapes.

validation.metric: Relation rows returned per GET /api/articles page and response bytes (Prisma query log in staging)
validation.expectation: Relation rows fall from sum(favorites+followers) on the page to at most one per relation per article; response size independent of popularity. Latency change unquantified until measured.
validation.falsifier: If relation rows are already at or below page size, impact was overstated; re-rank to P3.
validation.guard: Unit test asserting findMany include uses filtered favoritedBy/followedBy

commands.command: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c 'SELECT "A" AS article_id, count(*) FROM "_UserFavorites" GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 5;'
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c 'SELECT "B" AS followed_user, count(*) FROM "_UserFollows" GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 5;'
commands.purpose: Size the largest follower lists (also run with "A")

findings.problem: take: Number(query.limit) || 10 and skip: Number(query.offset) || 0 pass client input to the query with no maximum, on /articles and /articles/feed.
findings.performance_principle: Bound all work set by input you do not control; the server owns the maximum cost of a request.

evidence.statement: Controller passes req.query directly; no validation middleware or rate limiter

findings.conditions: One caller sending a large limit or offset, independent of traffic volume; severity grows with total article count (assumed growing). A gateway capping parameters would bound it.

counter_evidence.statement: Looked for Prisma/Express default maximum: none exists
Looked for gateway/proxy config in repo: none present

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If the deployment is private or behind a parameter-capping gateway and the table is small, the worst case is a slow but harmless response.
findings.recommendation: Clamp limit to a server maximum and reject negative/non-numeric offset in getArticles and getFeed; consider keyset pagination on (createdAt, id) if deep paging is observed.

alternatives.why: Removes the unbounded case at the source; trivial; no change for well-behaved clients

findings.trade_offs: Clients relying on very large pages are truncated; choosing MAX is a product decision.

validation.metric: articles.length and response bytes for an oversized limit
validation.expectation: articles.length <= MAX regardless of requested limit
validation.falsifier: If an oversized request already returns <= MAX, the finding is refuted.
validation.guard: Unit test calling getArticles({limit:'1000000'}) asserting take <= MAX

commands.purpose: Show response scales with table size, not page size (local seeded DB)

findings.problem: GET /articles/:slug/comments returns every visible comment, each with its author's full follower list; no take.
findings.performance_principle: Bound list responses on the server.
findings.conditions: Articles with hundreds or more comments; comment distribution unknown. RealWorld spec defines this endpoint unpaginated.

counter_evidence.statement: Visibility filter (author.demo OR author.id = me) partially bounds rows returned
Spec-defined unpaginated shape explains the design

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Articles may rarely exceed a few dozen comments, and the visibility filter further limits rows.
findings.recommendation: Add an optional server-capped limit ordered by createdAt; fix per-comment follower load via PERF-001.

alternatives.why: Bounds worst case while compatible for typical articles

findings.trade_offs: Possible truncation for spec clients expecting all comments.

validation.metric: Rows returned for the most-commented article
validation.expectation: Response row count never exceeds the cap
validation.falsifier: If no article exceeds the cap, the fix has no current effect.

commands.command: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c 'SELECT "articleId", count(*) FROM "Comment" GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 5;'

findings.problem: No index on Comment.articleId, Article.authorId, or Article.createdAt; comments list filters by articleId, feed filters by authorId, all lists ORDER BY createdAt DESC LIMIT.
findings.performance_principle: A predicate or sort over a growing table needs an access path proportional to the result, not the table.

evidence.statement: Initial migration creates only PKs, unique slug/email/username, and join-table indexes; later migrations add none
Feed filters articles by author's followers

findings.conditions: Matters once Comment/Article exceed cheap-scan size (roughly tens of thousands of rows). Both are append-only with no retention; current size unknown, so confidence capped at Medium.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched all four migrations for CREATE INDEX on these columns: none
At seed scale (144 articles, 1,728 comments) a sequential scan is optimal

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: On small tables sequential scans are optimal and indexes add write cost for nothing.
findings.recommendation: Add @@index([articleId]) on Comment and @@index([authorId]) / @@index([createdAt]) (or composite [authorId, createdAt]) on Article, chosen from EXPLAIN; build CONCURRENTLY on large tables.

alternatives.why: Directly provides access paths at small, understood cost

findings.trade_offs: Extra insert cost and storage; non-concurrent build blocks writes.

validation.metric: Plan node type and buffers; seq_scan vs idx_scan deltas in pg_stat_user_tables
validation.expectation: Seq Scan on Comment becomes index scan on articleId; list sort becomes index-ordered with early LIMIT
validation.falsifier: Planner still chooses seq scans after ANALYZE (tables too small): drop indexes, demote to P3.
validation.guard: Migration test/CI check that indexes exist; monitor idx_scan

commands.command: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c 'SELECT relname, seq_scan, seq_tup_read, idx_scan, n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY seq_tup_read DESC;'
commands.purpose: See scan pattern and table sizes

commands.command: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c 'EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM "Article" ORDER BY "createdAt" DESC LIMIT 10;'
commands.purpose: Actual rows examined for the sort (run on a replica)

findings.problem: Every list and feed request runs an exact prisma.article.count over the full filtered set, awaited serially before the independent findMany (also getArticles:71).
findings.performance_principle: Avoid whole-set aggregation for per-request metadata and do not serialize independent I/O.
findings.conditions: Matching articles in the many thousands with frequent list traffic; both unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: RealWorld spec requires articlesCount; limits recommendation, not mechanism
Count is trivial at seed scale

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Counts over a few thousand rows are cheap; the serial round trip is a small constant locally.
findings.recommendation: Issue count and page query concurrently (Promise.all or $transaction); consider has-more or approximate count only if measured expensive.

alternatives.why: Removes a serial round trip without contract change

findings.trade_offs: Two pool connections per request concurrently; $transaction holds a transaction.

validation.metric: pg_stat_statements mean_exec_time of the count query; query-log overlap in staging
validation.expectation: Queries overlap after change; count cost known
validation.falsifier: Count mean time negligible relative to list query: no count redesign needed.

findings.problem: GET /tags orders all tags by article _count (filtered by author demo/self) on every request; take:10 bounds output, not work.
findings.performance_principle: Do not recompute a whole-table aggregate per request when the result changes slowly.

evidence.statement: findMany with orderBy articles._count and relation filter

findings.conditions: _ArticleToTag large and /tags called on every page view (assumed); both unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Join table indexed on (A,B) and B; only the grouping is whole-set

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: At modest counts this is a fast aggregate.
findings.recommendation: Measure via pg_stat_statements; if significant, precompute demo-author tag popularity periodically and merge the caller's own tags per request.

alternatives.why: Removes repeated whole-set work with explicit staleness budget

findings.trade_offs: Refresh job and staleness; per-user term needs separate handling.

validation.metric: pg_stat_statements calls and mean_exec_time for the tag query
validation.expectation: Per-request query becomes a point read after change
validation.falsifier: Mean time already negligible: no action.

findings.problem: bcryptjs (pure JS, cost 10) runs hashing on the main thread of the single Node process in login, createUser, updateUser.
findings.performance_principle: CPU-bound work must not share the thread that services all I/O.
findings.conditions: Login/registration bursts coinciding with read traffic on the same process; login rate unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Async API yields between chunks; loop is saturated, not fully blocked
Hashing is necessary work; only its placement is at issue

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If logins are infrequent relative to reads, main-thread CPU share is negligible.
findings.recommendation: Measure event-loop delay during a login burst; if material, switch to native bcrypt/argon2 on the libuv pool.

alternatives.why: Moves CPU off the loop; bcrypt keeps hash format

findings.trade_offs: Native build tooling in Alpine; libuv pool contention (default 4).

validation.metric: perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay p99 during scripted login loop in staging
validation.expectation: Lag during logins falls after change

findings.problem: No request duration, per-route rate, query timing, pool wait, or event-loop lag measurement; PrismaClient has no log options.
findings.performance_principle: An unmeasured system cannot have bottlenecks confirmed or fixes validated.
findings.conditions: Any traffic level; matters as soon as PERF-001..007 need prioritizing or validating.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for logging/metrics libraries, /metrics routes, Prisma $on('query'): none; platform-level logs unknown

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: A hosting platform may provide edge request latency, though not query or event-loop data.
findings.recommendation: Add per-route request duration, monitorEventLoopDelay export, Prisma query logging/metrics in staging, and pg_stat_statements.

alternatives.why: Cheap and answers the open workload questions

findings.trade_offs: Small per-request overhead; log volume and cost.

validation.metric: Presence and population of route-latency and event-loop-delay series
validation.falsifier: Not applicable beyond presence check; series absent means not done.

findings.problem: One node process, no cluster/worker count, --max-old-space-size, UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE, or Prisma connection_limit; floating node:lts-alpine tag.
findings.performance_principle: Capacity configuration should be explicit and match provisioned resources.

evidence.statement: new PrismaClient() with no pool configuration

findings.conditions: Only if production gives one container multiple cores and runs a single container; unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Horizontal scaling with many single-process containers is valid and not visible here

findings.recommendation: Document intended process/instance count, pin Node major, and set connection_limit so instances x pool stays within max_connections.
findings.trade_offs: More processes multiply DB connections and memory.

validation.metric: Container CPU allotment vs process count in deployment config
validation.falsifier: Deployment already runs N one-core containers.

findings.problem: updateArticle issues four sequential statements (findFirst, optional findFirst, tag reset update, final update with per-tag connectOrCreate) plus relation reloads; tag list uncapped.
findings.performance_principle: Collapse dependent writes into one round trip or transaction and bound per-item write work.
findings.conditions: Writes assumed far less frequent than reads; material only with large tag lists.

counter_evidence.statement: Slug lookups hit the unique index; each step is cheap

findings.recommendation: Use tagList {set: [], connectOrCreate: [...]} in one update or wrap in $transaction; cap tag count; rely on unique constraint (P2002) instead of slug pre-check.
findings.trade_offs: Error handling moves to constraint-violation mapping.

validation.metric: Statements per article update in staging query log
validation.expectation: Falls from four plus one per tag to one transaction
validation.falsifier: Query log shows Prisma already merges the statements.

considered_not_reported.revisit_when: New code calls new PrismaClient() inside handlers

considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Prisma 4 batches each relation level into one query; real cost is row volume (PERF-001)

considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Bounded by body-parser default limit; no override
